title: Mean Value Theorem
subtitle: Where a tangent matches the average slope

slides.title: Same height at both ends
slides.text: This curve starts and ends at the same height. The dashed line joins the two ends, and it is flat. Drag the point until its tangent line is **parallel** to the dashed line.
slides.after: Found it: at $c$ ≈ {c} the tangent line is flat, so $f'(c)$ = 0.

slides.text: Could a smooth curve start and end at the same height, yet **never** have a flat tangent line in between?
options: No. Somewhere it has to turn around, and there the tangent is flat.
Yes, if it keeps going up the whole time.
Yes, if it is a straight line.
slides.hint: To get back to the starting height, what does a curve that went up have to do?
slides.explain: If it goes up, it must come back down to end at the same height. Where it turns around, the tangent is flat. (A horizontal straight line is flat everywhere.)

slides.title: More than one
slides.text: Same idea, wavier curve. There is more than one place where the tangent is flat. Find them all.
slides.found: Flat at $c$ ≈ {c}. There is another one. Keep looking.

slides.text:
**Rolle's Theorem**
If $f$ is **continuous** on $[a, b]$, **differentiable** on $(a, b)$, and $f(a) = f(b)$, then there is at least one $c$ in $(a, b)$ where $f'(c) = 0$.

How many conditions must $f$ meet before the theorem promises anything?
slides.explain: Continuous on $[a, b]$, differentiable on $(a, b)$, and equal heights at the ends.

slides.text: $f(x) = |x| - 1$ on $[-1, 1]$. Both ends are at height 0, but there is **no** flat tangent anywhere. Which condition of Rolle's Theorem fails?
slides.hint: Look at the sharp point at $x = 0$.
slides.explain: The corner at $x = 0$ has no derivative. Rolle's Theorem only works for functions that are differentiable on $(a, b)$.

slides.title: Use Rolle's Theorem
slides.text: $f(x) = 2x^2 - 4x + 5$ on $[-1, 3]$. First check the heights at the ends, then find $c$ with $f'(c) = 0$.
slides.explain: The ends match (both 11), the polynomial is smooth, and $4c - 4 = 0$ gives $c = 1$.

slides.text: $g(x) = 1 + frac{1}{x}$ on $[frac{1}{2}, 2]$. Does Rolle's Theorem apply?
slides.explain: $g(1/2) = 3$ but $g(2) = 1.5$. The heights don't match, so Rolle's Theorem says nothing. ($1/x$ is fine on this interval since 0 is not in it.)

slides.title: Try
slides.text: $f(x) = x^3 - 4x$ on $[-2, 2]$. Find **every** $c$ that Rolle's Theorem promises. Use the calculator if you need it.
slides.label: $c$ =

slides.title: Now tilt it
slides.text: This time the ends are at **different** heights. The dashed **secant line** joins them. Find every point where the tangent line is parallel to the secant line.
slides.found: Parallel at $c$ ≈ {c}. There is another one.
slides.after: Parallel at $c$ ≈ {c}. Both found: two places where the tangent matches the secant.

slides.text:
**Mean Value Theorem**
If $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ and differentiable on $(a, b)$, then there is at least one $c$ in $(a, b)$ where
$f'(c) = frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}$

What does $frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}$ measure?
options: The slope of the secant line through the two ends
The slope of the tangent line at $a$
slides.hint: Rise over run between which two points?
slides.explain: Rise $f(b) - f(a)$ over run $b - a$: the slope of the secant line. The MVT says some tangent line has that same slope.

slides.text: Compare the two theorems. Which condition from Rolle's Theorem does the Mean Value Theorem **drop**?
slides.hint: In the last picture, were the ends at the same height?
slides.explain: The MVT lets the ends sit at different heights. Rolle's Theorem is the special case where the secant line is flat.

slides.title: Find the $c$
slides.text: $f(x) = sqrt(x)$ on $[0, 9]$. Find the secant slope, then the $c$ the MVT guarantees.
slides.hint: Secant slope: $frac{sqrt(9) - sqrt(0)}{9 - 0}$. Then solve $frac{1}{2sqrt(c)} = frac{1}{3}$.

slides.title: Check it on the graph
slides.text: Drag the point to your answer and see if the tangent lines up with the secant.
slides.after: Right at $c$ = 2.25 the tangent is parallel to the secant.

slides.title: A road trip
slides.text: You drive to Grandma's house, 60 miles away, and it takes exactly 1 hour. What was your **average** speed?
slides.label: mph =

slides.text: What does the Mean Value Theorem tell you about the trip?
options: At some moment your speedometer read exactly 60 mph
You drove 60 mph the whole time
You never went faster than 60 mph
slides.hint: Average speed is the secant slope. Speedometer speed is the tangent slope.
slides.explain: Position is continuous and differentiable, so at some instant your instantaneous speed equaled your average speed. (Police use this: two speed cameras miles apart can prove you sped.)

slides.title: Drop a rock
slides.text: A rock is dropped from 100 ft. Its height is $s(t) = -16t^2 + 100$ feet after $t$ seconds.
slides.hint: It hits the ground when $s(t) = 0$: $16t^2 = 100$. Average velocity = $frac{s(2.5) - s(0)}{2.5 - 0}$.
slides.explain: $t^2 = 6.25$, so $t = 2.5$ s. Average velocity = $frac{0 - 100}{2.5}$ = −40 ft/s (negative: falling).

slides.title: When is it going its average speed?
slides.text: Here is the rock's height. The dashed line has slope −40, its average velocity. Find the moment its velocity, $s'(c)$, matches.
slides.after: At $t$ = {c} seconds the rock is falling at exactly 40 ft/s, its average speed. Check: $s'(t) = -32t$ = −40 gives $t$ = 1.25.

slides.title: Try
slides.text: Find the $c$ from the MVT for $f(x) = 2x^2 - 3x + 1$ on $[0, 2]$.
Suppose $f'(x) = 0$ at **every** $x$ in an interval. Use the MVT on any two points $a$ and $b$ there. What must be true about $f$?
options: $f$ is a line that is not flat
slides.hint: The MVT says $frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}$ equals some $f'(c)$. What is every $f'(c)$?
slides.explain: Every secant slope equals some $f'(c) = 0$, so $f(b) = f(a)$ for any two points. $f$ is constant. (Constant, not necessarily 0.)

slides.text: Suppose $f'(x) = g'(x)$ for every $x$ in an interval. Which must be true?
slides.hint: Apply the last result to $f - g$. What is its derivative?
slides.explain: $(f - g)' = 0$, so $f - g$ is constant. Same slopes everywhere means one graph is the other shifted up or down. This will matter a lot for antiderivatives.

slides.text: If f′(x) > 0 for every x in (a, b), then f is ___ on [a, b]. If f′(x) < 0, then f is ___.
slides.explain: Positive derivative: increasing. Negative derivative: decreasing. The MVT is what proves it.

slides.title: Theorem roundup
slides.text: You now know four big theorems. Match each one with what it promises.
pairs: $f$ has an absolute max and min on $[a, b]$
a local max or min at $c$ (where $f'(c)$ exists) has $f'(c) = 0$
some $c$ in $(a, b)$ has $f'(c) = frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}$
slides.hint: Rolle's and the MVT both promise a $c$; only one of them promises a flat tangent.
slides.explain: EVT: a max and min exist. Fermat: extremes have flat tangents. Rolle: a flat tangent. MVT: a tangent parallel to the secant.

slides.text: What does the **Mean Value Theorem** require of $f$?
slides.hint: Two conditions. Rolle's needs one more.
slides.explain: Continuous on the closed interval and differentiable on the open interval. That's all.

questions.text: Match each theorem with its **conclusion**.
pairs: $f$ has an absolute max and min on $[a, b]$
a local max or min at $c$ (where $f'(c)$ exists) has $f'(c) = 0$
some $c$ in $(a, b)$ has $f'(c) = frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}$
questions.explain: Each theorem's promise.

questions.text: Match each theorem with the **conditions** it needs.
pairs: $f$ continuous on a closed interval $[a, b]$
continuous on $[a, b]$, differentiable on $(a, b)$, and $f(a) = f(b)$
continuous on $[a, b]$ and differentiable on $(a, b)$
a local max or min at $c$, and $f$ differentiable at $c$
questions.explain: Rolle's needs exactly the MVT's conditions plus equal heights at the ends.

questions.text: Match each picture-description with the theorem it shows.
pairs: A flat tangent somewhere between two equal heights
A tangent line parallel to the secant line
A highest and lowest point on a closed interval
The tangent at a hilltop is flat
questions.explain: Rolle: flat tangent. MVT: tangent ∥ secant. EVT: the max and min exist. Fermat: extremes have $f' = 0$.

questions.text: Which conditions does **Rolle's Theorem** require?
questions.explain: Continuous, differentiable, and equal heights at the ends.

questions.text: Which conditions does the **Extreme Value Theorem** require?
questions.explain: Only continuity on a closed interval. No derivatives needed.

questions.text: Rolle's Theorem: if f is continuous on [a, b], differentiable on (a, b), and f(a) = ___, then some c in (a, b) has f′(c) = ___.
questions.explain: Equal heights at the ends give a flat tangent somewhere in between.

questions.text: Rolle's Theorem is the special case of the Mean Value Theorem where $f(a) = f(b)$.
questions.explain: With equal heights the secant is flat, so "parallel to the secant" means flat.

questions.text: The Mean Value Theorem says some tangent line is parallel to the secant line through $(a, f(a))$ and $(b, f(b))$.
questions.explain: Equal slopes mean parallel lines.

questions.text: The Mean Value Theorem tells you exactly where $c$ is.
questions.explain: It only promises that some $c$ exists. You find it yourself by solving $f'(c)$ = the secant slope.

questions.text: The Mean Value Theorem guarantees exactly one $c$.
questions.explain: **At least** one. The wavy cubic in the lesson had two.

questions.text: If $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ and $f(a) = f(b)$, there must be a $c$ with $f'(c) = 0$.
questions.explain: It also needs to be differentiable. $|x| - 1$ on $[-1, 1]$ has equal ends and no flat tangent.

questions.text: Does the MVT apply to $f(x) = |x|$ on $[-1, 2]$?
questions.explain: The corner at 0 has no derivative.

questions.text: Does the MVT apply to $f(x) = 1/x$ on $[-1, 1]$?
questions.explain: $1/x$ is undefined at 0. (The MVT doesn't need equal ends.)

questions.text: Does the MVT apply to $f(x) = x^2$ on $[0, 3]$?
questions.explain: Polynomials are continuous and differentiable everywhere. Equal ends are not required.

questions.text: Does Rolle's Theorem apply to $f(x) = x^(2/3)$ on $[-1, 1]$?
questions.explain: $f(-1) = f(1) = 1$, but the graph has a cusp at 0 where $f'$ does not exist.

questions.text: Does the MVT apply to $tan x$ on $[0, pi]$?
options: No: $tan x$ is not continuous at $pi/2$
questions.explain: $tan x$ has a vertical asymptote at $pi/2$.

questions.text: A car passes two speed cameras 3 miles apart, 2 minutes apart. What can the police conclude?
options: At some instant the car was going exactly 90 mph
The car went 90 mph the whole time
The car never went over 90 mph
questions.explain: 3 miles in 1/30 hour is 90 mph on average. By the MVT the speedometer read 90 at some instant.

questions.text: If $f'(x) = 0$ for every $x$ in an interval, then $f$ is constant there.
questions.explain: A corollary of the MVT.

questions.text: If $f'(x) = g'(x)$ for every $x$, then $f(x) = g(x)$.
questions.explain: Only $f = g + C$. For example $x^2$ and $x^2 + 5$.

questions.text: Which theorem is used to prove the Mean Value Theorem?
questions.explain: Tilt the picture: subtract the secant line from $f$ and apply Rolle's Theorem.

questions.text: Rolle's Theorem is proved by combining which two theorems?
options: The Extreme Value Theorem and Fermat's Theorem
questions.explain: The EVT gives a max or min inside the interval; Fermat says the tangent there is flat.

questions.text: In the MVT, $c$ must be…
questions.explain: $c$ is in the open interval $(a, b)$.

questions.explain: Secant slope = (9 − 1)/2 = 4. $2c = 4$ gives $c = 2$.

questions.explain: Secant slope = $frac{1 - 0}{e - 1}$. $1/c = 1/(e - 1)$ gives $c = e - 1 ≈ 1.7183$.
